item.title: What shapes the bright end of the UV luminosity function? Stellar mass, star-formation variability, and dust in JADES
item.description:
Amanda Stoffers, Sandro Tacchella, Benjamin D. Johnson, Brant Robertson, Roberto Maiolino, Andrew J. Bunker, Emma Curtis-Lake, A. Lola Danhaive, Qiao Duan, Francesco D'Eugenio

JWST surveys find more UV-bright galaxies at z>10 than galaxy-formation models predict, but the roles of recent star formation, stellar mass and dust remain uncertain. We analyse 1365 spectroscopically confirmed JADES galaxies at 3≤ z≤9, fitting NIRCam photometry and NIRSpec emission lines with \ceri. Our model includes flexible star-formation histories (SFHs) under three priors, two-component dust attenuation and nebular emission. We account for spectroscopic selection through population reweighting and assess the reliability of inferred trends. At z=3–5, rising SFHs are more common in low-mass galaxies, whereas most galaxies above 10^9.5 M⊙ have declining SFHs. The apparent increase in rising fractions with redshift cannot be distinguished from the adopted SFH prior alone. At fixed stellar mass, recent star formation is the strongest predictor of UV brightness. UV-brighter galaxies have higher recent SFRs, younger stellar populations and less attenuation at fixed SFR. Below 10^9 M⊙, they are also more likely to have rising SFHs, with odds increasing by up to a factor of 2.3 per magnitude brighter, although the strongest trend requires caution. In contrast, galaxies with M_UV<-20 at z=3–5 are predominantly massive, and approximately half have declining SFHs. Dust partly offsets burst-driven UV brightening: attenuation increases with recent SFR and declines gradually after the inferred SFR peak. In model sensitivity tests, dust has the largest effect on bright-end counts, whereas removing galaxy-to-galaxy SFH scatter changes them by at most 0.17~dex. Thus, bursts can make low-mass galaxies unusually UV-bright for their mass, while the absolute bright end of the UVLF is primarily shaped by stellar mass and dust attenuation.

item.title: The Role of Star Formation and Morphology in the Mass-Metallicity Relation of Galaxies at Cosmic Noon
item.description:
Farhanul Hasan, Marc Rafelski, Kalina V. Nedkova, Peter J. Watson, Debra M. Elmegreen, Bruce G. Elmegreen, Zahra Sattari, Vihang Mehta, Alaina Henry, Mitchell Revalski, Benedetta Vulcani, Grecco A. Oyarzun, Y. Sophia Dai, Xin Wang, Matthew A. Malkan, Claudia M. Scarlata, Matthew J. Hayes, Alexandra Le Reste, Andrew J. Battisti, Anahita Alavi, James Colbert, Hakim Atek, Michael Rutkowski, Tucker Jones, Ilias Goovaerts, Alexander Beckett, Andrew J. Bunker, Mason Huberty

We investigate the dependence of the mass-metallicity relation (MZR) on star formation and galaxy morphology at 1.7<z<3.5, using JWST/NIRISS wide-field slitless spectroscopy of >1000 galaxies. The observations span >85 arcmin2 from the pure-parallel PASSAGE and OutThere surveys. We derive gas-phase metallicities using a Bayesian framework that combines multiple strong emission-line ratios calibrated against direct auroral-line metallicity measurements from JWST. We constrain stellar masses, star formation rates (SFRs), and morphological properties using ancillary HST and JWST imaging. We stack spectra by stellar mass to constrain the MZR over log(M✶/M)~6.5-11, and find that it is well described by a second-order polynomial, with a steep low-mass slope and metallicities<10% solar at log(M✶/M)<7.5. Additional stacking by SFR and morphology reveals strong evidence for a fundamental metallicity relation (FMR). Specifically, at log(M✶/M)<9.5, galaxies with lower SFRs are more metal-rich than those with higher SFRs at fixed mass. At log(M✶/M)<9.5, we find that larger galaxies, and those having lower SFR surface densities, bulges, and/or spiral features are significantly metal rich relative to their smaller, higher SFR surface density, bulge-less, and/or non-spiral counterparts. These results suggest the secondary dependencies of the MZR reflect variations in the baryon cycle, such that recent metal-poor gas accretion drives concentrated star formation and metallicity dilution, while structurally developed galaxies retain more chemically enriched gas reservoirs.

item.title: Little Red Dots with Broad Hβ Lines Reveal the Black Hole Mass Function at 7<z<9.5
item.description:
Anthony J. Taylor, Steven L. Finkelstein, Hollis B. Akins, Vasily Kokorev, Pablo Arrabal Haro, Sophie Koudmani, Caitlin M. Casey, Mark Dickinson, Junehyoung Jeon, Madisyn Brooks, Volker Bromm, Christopher J. Conselice, Kelcey Davis, Callum T. Donnan, Andreas L. Faisst, Seiji Fujimoto, Lukas J. Furtak, Mauro Giavalisco, Ansh R. Gupta, Michaela Hirschmann, Tiger Yu-Yang Hsiao, Dale D. Kocevski, Anton M. Koekemoer, Gene C. K. Leung, Ray A. Lucas, Lorenzo Napolitano, Casey Papovich, Laura Pentericci, Pablo G. Perez-Gonzalez, Rachel S. Somerville, Fabian Walter, L. Y. Aaron Yung

We present a systematic search for broad Hβ emission at 7<z<9.5 in 21,770 JWST/NIRSpec PRISM spectra drawn from four blank fields and six lensing clusters with photometry spanning 1942 arcmin2. We find a sample of 20 sources with statistically significant broad-Hβ emission, including 13 new sources. Our entire sample has colors and morphologies consistent with little red dots (LRDs), compared to only 37% of broad-line emitters at 3.5<z<6. Interpreting the broad-lines as indicators of Broad-line Active Galactic Nuclei (BLAGN), we infer black hole masses of 4.2×10^6-2.1×10^8 M⊙. We calculate completeness corrections and construct the black hole mass function at z~8. The normalization of the black hole mass function rises by ≈1.0~dex from z~8-5, consistent with average black hole growth at f_rmEdd≈0.1. Comparing with cosmological simulations, the z~8 black hole mass function requires heavy (10^5 M⊙) seeds or super-Eddington accretion onto light or intermediate mass seeds to match its normalization. Finally, we infer bolometric luminosities for the sample and construct a bolometric luminosity function. We integrate over this luminosity function to derive a black hole accretion density (BHAD) of 4.8^+5.8_-2.6×10^-7~M⊙~rmyr^-1~rmMpc^-3, showing broad agreement with previous photometric work, but disagreement with previous X-ray models, reinforcing the idea that BLAGN are more common in the early universe than previously expected.

item.title: JWST/MIRI Observations of Amorphous Silicates in Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS
item.description:
Cristina A. Thomas, Michael S. P. Kelley, David E. Harker, Martin A. Cordiner, Davide Farnocchia, Dennis Bodewits, Steven B. Charnley, Maria N. Drozdovskaya, Marco Micheli, Stefanie N. Milam, Cyrielle Opitom, Silvia Protopapa, Nathan X. Roth, Megan E. Schwamb

We present JWST/MIRI Low Resolution Spectroscopy (LRS) of 3I/ATLAS obtained post-perihelion at a heliocentric distance of 2.21 au. Our spectrum contains a prominent 10 micron silicate emission feature with a broad, smooth shape that is distinct from those commonly observed in Solar System comets. We model the spectrum using thermal emission from amorphous carbon, amorphous olivine, and amorphous pyroxene grains. Our models strongly favor a pyroxene-dominated, amorphous silicate composition and show a degeneracy between silicate grain size and the relative abundance of silicate and carbon dust. Across a set of representative models, the best-fitting crystalline abundance is zero, and we place an upper limit of 5.3% on the crystalline fraction of the silicates. We identify an emission feature near 6.83 microns that is consistent with aliphatic C-H-bearing material. The overwhelmingly amorphous silicate composition supports previous work that measured unusual volatile and isotopic composition in suggesting that the material incorporated into the object experienced little thermal processing and preserves information about the conditions in which this interstellar planetesimal formed.

item.title: Excitation and Destruction of Small Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons by the Luminous Seyfert Nucleus of NGC 4151
item.description:
Grant P. Donnelly, J. -D. T. Smith, Sebastian F. Hönig, Daniel A. Dale, Tanio Díaz-Santos, B. T. Draine, Brandon S. Hensley, Thomas S. -Y. Lai, Karin M. Sandstrom, Andrey Vayner

We present a spatially-resolved detection of 3.3 μm emission from polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) within the circumnuclear ~200 pc of the archetypal Seyfert galaxy NGC 4151, using new JWST NIRSpec/IFU spectroscopy. PAHs are detected down to the innermost 50 pc, though it is likely that PAHs also exist at smaller radii, as PAH detections closer than this seem to be limited by continuum dilution. This is contrary to expectations that PAH grains, especially the smallest grains that carry the 3.3 μm feature, could not survive near an active galactic nucleus (AGN). Furthermore, the surface brightness of PAH emission increases as radius from the nucleus decreases. We interpret this as evidence that the AGN supplies energy for PAH excitation by driving ultraviolet emission in nearby H and H2 gas. We do not detect PAH emission within the narrow line region (NLR) that hosts highly ionized and outflowing gas, suggesting that the AGN may also destroy PAHs in these regions, depending on geometry. Together, these results show that an AGN has a complex, multifaceted role in the life cycle of PAHs and in PAH excitation.

item.title: A Collimated Protostellar Outflow Likely Driven by Jet and Reshaped by Environment in the Sagittarius C Cloud of the Central Molecular Zone
item.description:
Sen-Di Bo, Xing Lu, Tian-Yu Tu, Weiyuan Zhang, Samuel Crowe, Junhao Liu, Shanghuo Li, John Bally

The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) at the center of the Galaxy provides a nearby laboratory for studying star formation under extreme physical and chemical conditions. Recent ALMA (Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array) observations have identified 43 candidate protostellar outflows in three CMZ clouds. One of these, the Sgr C-F#2 outflow in Sagittarius C (Sgr C), has a highly collimated lobe extending approximately 0.8 pc in projection. Here we present a joint analysis of ALMA observations of SiO J=8-7, 5-4, and 2-1. We use local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) and non-LTE methods to constrain the SiO column densities, H2 number density, and gas temperature. The low SiO rotational temperatures and higher kinetic temperatures inferred from non-LTE methods suggest subthermal excitation. The elongated SiO morphology, shock-excited gas, position-velocity structure, and the alignment of the red shifted molecular lobe with JWST infrared knots altogether favor jet-dominated entrainment, whereas a broader disk-wind component close to the source cannot be excluded. The outflow shows asymmetries in its morphology and physical properties, which can be attributed to dense gas on the path of its lobe impeding its propagation and feedback from a nearby HII region imposing different pressure on its two sides.

item.title: Heavy Seeds and the Multi-scale Fueling of Early Supermassive Black Holes and Little Red Dots
item.description:
Junehyoung Jeon, Volker Bromm, Boyuan Liu, Stella S. R. Offner, Anthony J. Taylor, Steven L. Finkelstein

The formation of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in the early Universe has been a longstanding mystery due to the brief period available to assemble them. More recently, the unexpected discovery with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) of Little Red Dots (LRDs), compact sources exhibiting signatures of active galactic nuclei (AGN), has accentuated this challenge. Cosmological simulations investigating their formation and evolution confront the limitation that the compact scale of SMBH/LRD physics cannot be simultaneously resolved with the larger-scale cosmological environment. We address this limitation by utilizing a cutout technique, selecting a targeted region around an SMBH seed from a cosmological parent simulation and re-running the cutout at higher (sub-pc) resolution for shorter periods. We explore two SMBH formation scenarios: the standard, light seed stellar-remnant case, and the heavy-seed, direct collapse black hole (DCBH) channel. Within the high-resolution achieved by the cutouts, the DCBH, due to its larger mass, is able to induce a buildup of high density gas nearby and accrete gas in bursts of super-Eddington phases, growing in mass and producing an LRD-like spectrum. In contrast, the stellar remnant cannot do so and remains dormant, unable to affect the nearby gas or significantly evolve by gas accretion alone. Therefore, we find that observed high-redshift SMBHs and LRDs require the existence of heavy seeds to assemble dense gas around themselves, enabling efficient growth and producing red optical spectra with strong Balmer breaks resembling LRDs.

item.title: Does the Escape Fraction Prescription Shape Reionization History and Morphology?
item.description:
Pulkit Sheoran, Ankita Bera, Sultan Hassan

The escape fraction of ionizing photons, fesc, is one of the least constrained quantities of the Epoch of Reionization (EoR), and the opacity of the intergalactic medium prevents its direct measurement at high redshifts. We constrain three power-law parameterizations, fesc(z), fesc(M_h), and fesc(z, M_h), against JWST UV luminosity functions and EoR observables (the ionizing emissivity, the neutral hydrogen fraction, and the Thomson optical depth) using Markov Chain Monte Carlo, with priors that allow fesc to either increase or decrease with redshift and halo mass. We then propagate the best-fit models into the semi-numerical simulation SimFast21 and compare their ionization morphology and 21 cm power spectra with those of a constant-fesc model. All models reproduce the observations with nearly identical global reionization histories. The data favor an escape fraction that decreases with increasing redshift, from ≈ 0.8 at z = 5 to ≈ 0.35 at z = 15. The halo-mass-only model prefers fesc increasing with halo mass, but this trend acts as a proxy for redshift evolution. When we vary both dependencies jointly, the data prefer a mass-independent fesc. At matched global neutral fraction, the ionization morphology is closely similar for all four prescriptions, and the 21 cm power spectra agree to within ≈ 10%. These results suggest that, once calibrated against the same observations, the details of the fesc prescription, which are set by the physics of the interstellar medium, largely average out in both the global observables and the 21 cm power spectrum. Distinguishing them may require statistics beyond the power spectrum, such as sightline statistics of the Lyα and 21 cm forests, or forecasts that exploit their small differences in reionization timing.

item.title: The Stellar Populations of Resolved Galaxies
item.description:
Daniel R. Weisz, Alessandro Savino, Evan D. Skillman

The study of galaxies outside the Milky Way using observations of resolved stellar populations has experienced extraordinary growth over the past two decades. There now exist panchromatic photometry and precise astrometry for hundreds of millions of individually resolved stars in hundreds of galaxies that span ~10^9 in luminosity, ~10^3 in metallicity, and sample a wide range of environments. Here, we review advances in extragalactic astronomy enabled by resolved stellar population imaging. We summarize major observational programs and focus on four interconnected science areas: the star formation histories of galaxies, 'bursty' star formation, the stellar initial mass function, and the orbital histories of Local Group galaxies. We review the literature in each area, synthesize key findings, identify emerging trends, and discuss how new and future facilities (e.g., JWST, LSST, Euclid, Roman, CSST, ELTs, HWO) will enable further progress. Finally, we highlight shortcomings in current datasets and discuss promising directions for new areas of investigation.

Backhaus, Micaela B. Bagley, Guillermo Barro, Laura Bisigello, Madisyn Brooks, Jaclyn B. Champagne, Yingjie Cheng, Nikko J. Cleri, Dan Coe, Luca Costantin, Alexander de la Vega, Mark Dickinson, Callum T. Donnan, Henry C. Ferguson, Eric Gawiser, Ananya Ganapathy, Giovanni Gandolfi, Mauro Giavalisco, Norman A. Grogin, Michaela Hirschmann, Weida Hu, Taylor A. Hutchison, Intae Jung, Jeyhan S. Kartaltepe, Dale D. Kocevski, Gene C. K. Leung, Mario Llerena, Ray A. Lucas, Faezeh Manesh, Elizabeth J. McGrath, Jessica A. Mitlehner, Casey Papovich, Pablo G. Pérez-González, Giulia Rodighiero, Raymond C. Simons, Lu Shen, Rachel S. Somerville, Brittany N. Vanderhoof, L. Y. Aaron Yung, Jorge A. Zavala

We present the Star-formation from Photometry through the Addition of Medium-bands (SPAM) survey, a 62.9 hr JWST/NIRCam imaging program to add ten new filters, nine medium-band filters, and one broad-band filter to the CEERS legacy dataset. We describe the observation strategy, present the data, and detail the data-reduction process. We include a complete reduction of imaging in the legacy CEERS footprint, inclusive of all publicly available photometric parallel and GO observations within the legacy CEERS footprint. We present a multi-band photometric and photometric redshift catalog which includes all medium- and broad-band filters available on NIRCam. We find that adding medium bands from the SPAM and MINERVA programs improves photometric redshifts. We discuss how these data advance the SPAM survey's key science goals: better-constrained photometric redshifts, identification of high-redshift overdensity members, improved recovery of emission-line strengths, and more accurate star formation histories.

item.title: Multiphase Gas Structure in JWST Little Red Dots
item.description:
Seok-Jun Chang, Max Gronke, Jorryt Matthee, Charlotte Mason

JWST has uncovered a population of compact high-redshift galaxies, 'little red dots' (LRDs), exhibiting broad Balmer emission lines that often show narrow absorption features and strong Balmer breaks - spectral signatures attributed to dense gas surrounding rapidly growing black holes, but whose small-scale structure remains unknown. A striking feature of LRD spectra is that the Hβ absorption is systematically deeper than Hα, yet in any homogeneous gas this ordering is physically impossible. Here we model the Hα and Hβ line profiles using radiative transfer simulations for 11 LRDs with JWST sensitive high resolution spectroscopy, and independently constrain the n=2 hydrogen column density, N_HI,\mathitn=2, from the Balmer-break continuum. We find that the N_HI,\mathitn=2 from Hα in a homogeneous medium cannot reproduce the observed Hβ absorption in several objects, and that this N_HI,\mathitn=2 typically falls two orders of magnitude below the lower bound set by the Balmer break. Both tensions are simultaneously resolved by a multiphase medium of dense clumps within diffuse hot ionized gas. This multiphase gas structure is a necessary ingredient for any viable LRD model, regardless of the nature of the central engine.

item.title: Theoretical Pulsation Properties of RR Lyrae and Type II Cepheids in the JWST and Roman photometric systems
item.description:
M. Marconi, R. Molinaro, A. Bhardwaj, I. Musella, V. Ripepi, E. Trentin, G. De Somma, T. Sicignano, M. Deka, M. Gholami, E. Luongo, M. Dall Ora, S. Leccia

RR Lyrae (RRL) stars and Type II Cepheids (T2Cs) are key standard candles and tracers of old stellar populations. The deep, wide-field capabilities of facilities such as the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will significantly expand their utility as a Population II alternative to Classical Cepheids for distance scale calibrations. We present theoretical pulsation properties-including light-curve morphologies, amplitudes, and multi-filter relations for RRLs (Z = 0.0001 - 0.02, M = 0.51 - 0.80, M⊙) and T2Cs (Z = 0.0001 - 0.01, M = 0.495 - 0.65, M⊙) to enable detailed studies of Galactic and extragalactic populations. Using alreday available non-linear convective pulsation models, we converted their predicted bolometric light curves across various chemical compositions and evolutionary stages into the JWST and Roman photometric systems. From these, we derived multi-filter Period-Amplitude and Color-Color diagrams, alongside Period-Luminosity and Period-Wesenheit relations with explicit metallicity terms. RRL relations display a significantly stronger zero-point metallicity dependence than those of T2Cs, despite sharing similar slopes. Consequently, T2Cs offer a distance scale indicator that is remarkably robust against metallicity uncertainties. As a preliminary test, we applied our metal-dependent Period-Wesenheit relations to a subset of JWST-observed RRLs in the WLM galaxy, deriving a distance modulus of mu_0 = 24.85 +/- 0.03 mag (assuming the literature average metallicity). The derived distance to WLM is consistent with most literature values, though slightly shorter than determinations based on Classical Cepheids and the Tip of the Red Giant Branch. These theoretical relations pave the way for future high-precision distance determinations and asteroseismic diagnostics with JWST and Roman.

item.title: Recently launched AGN-driven outflow in a lensed quiescent galaxy at Cosmic Noon
item.description:
Letizia Bugiani, Andrew B. Newman, Sirio Belli, Cosimo Marconcini, Pietro Bergamini, Sai Gangula, Claudio Grillo, Andrea Bolamperti, Katherine E. Whitaker, Aliza Beverage, Richard S. Ellis, Amir H. Khoram, Allison Matthews, Marco Lombardi

We analyze JWST/NIRSpec IFU spectroscopy of MRG-M0150, a gravitationally lensed, massive quiescent galaxy at z=2.6 from the INQUEST-JWST survey. Thanks to the combination of lensing magnification with JWST's angular resolution, we are able to build spatially resolved maps of the ionized gas spatial distribution, kinematics, and ionization properties in this system. We detect ionized gas emission throughout the galaxy: the lack of residual star formation inferred from line-ratio diagnostic diagrams, together with the decoupling between the gas and stellar kinematics, suggest that the ionized gas is in a wind. We use the 3D gas kinematics modeling code ttMOKA3D to constrain the geometry and physical properties of the ionized gas wind. We find that the observations are consistent with a biconical wind driven by the low-luminosity AGN at the center of the galaxy, which is detected in X-rays. The wind reaches high velocities of 1000-1400 km/s, implying that part of the gas may escape the halo. The ionized gas mass outflow rate, (0.6 ± 0.2)~M⊙~yr^-1, is modest but exceeds the upper limit on the residual star formation rate, and it is likely that the wind is multiphase and carries more mass. We show that typical unresolved observations would not detect the wind, suggesting that the incidence of such outflows may be higher than previously recognized. Simple geometric arguments show that the observed outflow must have been launched ≈ 0.45~Myr ago from the time of observation. This evidence suggests that low-level AGN activity is an important mechanism for maintaining quiescence in massive galaxies at cosmic noon, potentially over cosmological timescales.

item.title: How Steep is your Dust? Direct Measurements of Nebular Attenuation Curves at Cosmic Noon with JWST
item.description:
Gabriel Maheson, Sirio Belli, Sandro Tacchella, Letizia Bugiani, Joel Leja, Rebecca Davies, Minjung Park, Amir H. Khoram, Matteo Sapori, Caterina Liboni, Benjamin P. Collins

Tracing the shape of the nebular attenuation curve, which is crucial for accurately measuring intrinsic emission-line fluxes, has proven challenging both in the local universe and at high redshift. Here we present nebular dust attenuation curves measured directly for 24 star-forming galaxies (9.3<log(M✶/M⊙)<11.1) at cosmic noon (1.8<z<3.3) from the Blue Jay survey. Using deep JWST/NIRSpec spectra, we measure up to eight hydrogen recombination lines from Hδ to Paβ per galaxy and find little diversity in the curve shape, with most galaxies agreeing with the \citetcalzetti_dust_2000 attenuation curve. For over 90% of the sample, the nebular reddening from the Balmer lines is consistent with that from the Paschen lines. Using ttProspector spectral energy distribution (SED) fits, we obtain the stellar reddening and find that the difference between stellar and nebular reddening increases with stellar mass, and that each reddening measurement is independent of inclination, which disagrees with the two-component dust model. We then measure the impact of using the derived nebular attenuation curve or a literature curve when determining metallicity using the strong-line method, and find that for some diagnostics (e.g., S32, S3, S23, and S3O3), the difference can be as large as 5σ. Caution is needed when using these diagnostics if the nebular attenuation curve cannot be directly measured, since the resulting uncertainty can exceed the measurement uncertainty on the emission-line fluxes even with high signal-to-noise Balmer decrement measurements. These results show that the shape of the nebular attenuation curve is poorly understood and that constraining it is important for reducing systematic uncertainty in galaxy measurements.

We present the discovery of supernova (SN) Ares, a strongly lensed supernova at zspec=1.276±0.002 in a massive, triply imaged host galaxy behind the MACS J0308.9+2645 galaxy cluster. item.title: A Composite Rest-Frame UV Spectrum of Galaxies at 5.7 < z < 6.9: Ionization, Outflows, and Implications for Intergalactic Metal Enrichment
item.description:

We present a stacked JWST/NIRSpec spectrum of 104 galaxies at λ_rest=1200–2000\mathringA to study nebular emission and absorption from the interstellar medium (ISM) and stellar winds. The sample is drawn from known [O III] emitters with mean redshift z=6.50, absolute UV magnitude M_UV=-20.7, and stellar mass M✶=10^8.93M⊙. Lyα has comparable strength and is redshifted relative to the [O III] systemic frame, consistent with production in gaseous outflows. High-ionization emission lines including O III], C III], and He II are slightly stronger than in lower-redshift stacks but exhibit narrow widths, disfavoring ionization from a broad-line AGN. Emission-line ratios slightly favor ionization by a hard stellar continuum, though a contribution from a narrow-line nuclear source cannot be strictly excluded. Numerous strong absorption lines at both high and low ionization are blueshifted by ~200km s-1, again indicating outflows driven by stellar winds or entrained metal-enriched ISM. A simple model suggests that at z~6.5 most star-forming galaxies are too young for winds at these velocities to propagate beyond ~3–9 proper kpc, implying that the observed [O III] emitter population alone cannot explain the frequency of heavy-element absorbers seen in quasar spectra. In this picture, early enrichment of the intergalactic medium likely arises from undetected low-mass galaxies (M✶~10^5–10^6M⊙) clustered around the more massive systems detected in JWST/NIRCam WFSS surveys.

item.title: Star clusters at cosmic dawn I: the emergence of the initial cluster mass function
item.description:
Fred S. Thompson, Julien Devriendt, Adrianne Slyz, Taysun Kimm, Cheonsu Kang

JWST observations of lensed galaxies reveal unusually bright star-cluster candidates within the first billion years after the Big Bang. However, the physical processes shaping the initial cluster mass function (ICMF) remain uncertain. We study the formation of a galaxy embedded in a dark matter halo whose virial mass reaches 10^10 M⊙ at z=6, using cosmological radiation-hydrodynamics zoom-in simulations. Its star clusters, represented by sink particles, accrete gas and form stellar populations that supply radiation and supernova feedback, thereby regulating their own growth. As we do not prescribe an efficiency per free-fall time or a fixed star-cluster formation duration, the ICMF emerges self-consistently. We assess the effects of numerical resolution and stellar radiation. Schechter fits to the central-galaxy ICMF give truncation masses near 6 × 10^6 M⊙, with substantial uncertainty. At fixed resolution, including stellar radiation makes the low-mass slope of the ICMF shallower, from -1.60 to -1.34, while doubling the spatial resolution steepens it back to -1.54. Stellar radiation also reduces the abundance of low-mass clouds, particularly those with lower gas densities, and shortens the formation time of star clusters to about a Myr, i.e. well before their first supernovae go off. On average, more rapidly fed star clusters accrete for longer, making their final masses rise faster than linearly with the initial accretion rate and contributing to a flatter ICMF. At fixed host-galaxy star formation rate, our brightest simulated clusters reach UV luminosities comparable to those of observed lensed star-cluster candidates.

item.description:

Our work utilises nine fields covering ~1,045~arcmin2 in total, including seven blank fields and two galaxy cluster fields. item.title: Not so Fast: Revised Calibration of SIDM Core Collapse
item.description:
Frank C. van den Bosch, Yarone M. Tokayer

Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) haloes undergo gravothermal evolution whose late-time behaviour is central to predictions for dense substructure and black-hole seed formation. We revisit the calibration of this evolution using a new spherical Direct Simulation Monte Carlo code, SphDSMC, which follows spherically symmetric SIDM systems without force softening and to substantially higher central densities than standard N-body simulations. We compare SphDSMC calculations with conventional N-body simulations and with one-dimensional gravothermal fluid models. We show that N-body results converge to SphDSMC only for softening lengths significantly smaller than those normally adopted for collisionless simulations, and that allowing multiple scatterings per particle per time step does not introduce significant errors when implemented appropriately. Calibrating the gravothermal fluid equations against SphDSMC, we find that the commonly used harmonic interpolation between the long- and short-mean-free-path conductivities is inaccurate. A gentler transition, however, yields excellent agreement for NFW haloes over a range of concentrations and truncation radii, with a single long-mean-free-path conductivity parameter. The revised calibration gives a long-mean-free-path collapse time that is somewhat shorter than previous estimates, but we show that collapse slows dramatically once the core becomes optically thick. We provide fitting functions for the late-time evolution and argue that black-hole seed formation by SIDM gravothermal collapse has generally been underestimated in duration, making it unlikely to explain the massive high-redshift black holes inferred from JWST observations without additional physics.

item.title: The Future of Gamma-Ray Bursts as Probes of the Epoch of Reionization in the Era of JWST and the Extremely Large Telescope
item.description:
H. M. Fausey, A. J. van der Horst, N. R. Tanvir, K. Wiersema

The Epoch of Reionization (EoR) is a key era of cosmological history that remains poorly understood. An examination of the Ly-alpha damping wing of high-redshift GRBs can provide direct measurements of the fraction of neutral hydrogen (i.e., neutral fraction) of the IGM in the vicinity of the GRB host galaxy, in addition to the neutral column in the host along the sight-line to the GRB. The latter quantity can help infer the fraction of ionizing photons escaping the galaxy (i.e. escape fraction); the average escape fraction being a key input to EoR models. New and upcoming observatories such as the JWST and the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) can obtain more robust estimates of the hydrogen column density and neutral fraction around high-redshift GRBs. We simulate spectra for the JWST NIRSpec and ELT HARMONI spectrographs using different GRB magnitudes and exposure times to determine their capabilities for measuring column densities and neutral fractions with the Ly-alpha damping wings of high-redshift GRBs. We find that both spectrographs will be highly effective for obtaining column density estimates. Despite the presence of telluric lines, we find that ELT HARMONI will be a powerful instrument for retrieving accurate neutral fraction estimates, but JWST NIRSpec will be vital for obtaining neutral fraction measurements for bright GRBs that fall in redshift ranges where ELT is less effective. Additionally, shorter JWST Target of Opportunity (ToO) follow-up times would greatly increase the accuracy of neutral fraction estimates obtained with NIRSpec spectra.

item.title: Consistently Reproducing Early Galaxy Observations and 21-cm Signal during the Epoch of Reionization
item.description:
Michele Bianco, Sambit K. Giri, Arghyadeep Basu, Tommaso Boschi, Aurel Schneider, Enrico Garaldi, Garrelt Mellema

In the standard cosmological model, galaxies forming within dark matter haloes are the primary drivers of the Epoch of Reionization (EoR). The complex physics of galaxy formation introduces scatter in the relation between halo mass and star-formation activity, with implications for the production and escape of ionising photons. In this work, we implement a stochastic source model in our cosmological radiative transfer simulations. We calibrate our model against the high-redshift ultraviolet luminosity function observed by JWST and observational constraints on Lyman-continuum leakage to constrain the ionising escape fraction. We find that stochastic star formation redistributes ionising emissivity toward lower-mass haloes, producing a more fragmented ionisation topology and delaying the growth of the largest ionised regions relative to the deterministic, observationally calibrated model. However, when the two models match total ionising photon production, their global neutral fractions and 21-cm power spectrum remain nearly indistinguishable, despite small differences in the morphology of individual ionised regions. Additionally, we establish a unified framework that lets us apply source models derived from computationally expensive hydrodynamical simulations (SPICE, FIRE-2 and Thesan) and investigate their impact on large-volume reionisation simulations, extending their prescriptions to scales of >100 Mpc. We find that these prescriptions produce distinct ionisation topologies and 21-cm statistical signatures, even when their global reionisation histories are similar. Our results highlight the importance of combining physically motivated galaxy formation prescriptions from hydrodynamical simulations with large-volume radiative transfer simulations to interpret forthcoming 21-cm observations and constrain the sources of cosmic reionisation.

item.title: Clustering of JWST LRDs. Implications for PBHs and other early-forming seeds
item.description:
Gert Hütsi

We use the observed abundance and spatial clustering of JWST little red dots (LRDs) over z = 4–8 to confront two formation scenarios: the standard picture in which LRDs form in virialized dark-matter halos, and one in which they are seeded by a dynamically subdominant population of primordial black holes (PBHs). The halo formation scenario accounts for both observables naturally and without fine-tuning. In the PBH scenario, matching the observed LRD abundance requires a negligibly small PBH mass fraction, and a power-spectrum analysis shows that such a Poisson isocurvature component predicts a clustering signal far below what is observed. The same conclusion holds for any population of dynamically subdominant early-forming seeds, unless their initial clustering is finely tuned or their activity is tied to massive host halos. We conclude that the spatial clustering of JWST LRDs strongly favours the standard halo formation picture and disfavours PBHs, or similar early-forming seeds, as a randomly activated LRD population; PBHs remain viable as seeds only if their activity is governed by massive host halos, in which case clustering alone cannot distinguish them from astrophysical seeds.

item.title: Dust in Galaxies at z=10-15: Attenuation and Re-emission Predictions from the FirstLight Simulations

Finally, it will enable probing the molecular gas kinematics and identify molecular outflows driven by supermassive black holes. When combined with the rich legacy of JWST, ELT, and SKAO surveys, ALMA2040 will deliver a comprehensive, multi-phase view of feedback and quenching, allowing us to establish when, how, and why galaxies shut down their star formation across cosmic time.

item.title: Are High-EW LAEs good analogs for the earliest galaxies? A study on the ionizing conditions and gas properties of LAEs at 2≲ z≲7
item.description:
Lena Pless, Themiya Nanayakkara, Karl Glazebrook, Michael Maseda, Jarle Brinchmann, Tanya Urrutia

Lyman-α emitters (LAEs) are frequently proposed as analogs of the low-mass, metal-poor galaxies thought to dominate cosmic reionization. In particular, galaxies with large Lyα equivalent widths (EWs) are expected to have not experienced significant chemical enrichment. We test this hypothesis using a sample of 88 LAEs at 2 ≲ z≲ 7, selected from MUSE observations that are undetected in deep HST imaging and subsequently followed up with JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy. Despite the unprecedented sensitivity of JWST, only 50 of the LAEs exhibit secure counterparts in available deep NIRCam imaging reaching typical 3σ depths of m_AB~30.3 mag, highlighting the intrinsically faint nature of the population. Gas-phase metallicities are inferred by fitting optical emission lines with a grid of BPASS+cloudy photoionization models, while stellar masses are derived from NIRCam photometry through SED fitting. The final sample with secure stellar masses and gas-phase metallicities encompasses only 16 LAEs, occupying regions of standard emission-line diagnostic diagrams consistent with low-metallicity star-forming systems. Although the strong-line metallicity diagnostic R3 appears to decrease with increasing EW, we find no compelling evidence for a strong monotonic relation between EW and gas-phase metallicity when metallicities are inferred through full emission-line fitting. However, galaxies with stronger Lyα emission tend to lie below the average mass-metallicity relation at fixed stellar masses, suggesting that they are preferentially less chemically evolved than typical galaxies of the same mass. We conclude that high-EW LAEs provide useful, though imperfect, analogs of the galaxies thought to drive cosmic reionization, and combining EW with stellar mass may provide a more effective route for identifying the most chemically primitive galaxies.

item.title: A machine-learning-driven dataset of 144,111 polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon infrared spectra for interpreting aromatic infrared bands
item.description:
Xinghong Mai, Zu-Jia Lu, Zhao Wang

The interpretation of interstellar aromatic infrared bands (AIBs) relies on reference spectral libraries, but the chemical space covered by existing databases remains incomplete relative to the vast structural diversity of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) expected in the interstellar medium. We present a large-scale, high-throughput PAH infrared (IR) spectral database that complements existing reference libraries by providing significantly more continuous coverage of the PAH chemical space for small to medium-sized PAHs. We used a machine-learning double-harmonic (ML-DH) framework that integrates neural network force fields with electronic dipole models. This framework achieves quantum-chemical accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. It has been validated against independent density functional theory calculations and benchmark spectral databases. The resulting dataset comprises 144,111 IR spectra for 48,037 closed-shell, even-carbon benzenoid PAH structures across neutral, cationic, and anionic charge states, complete with per-spectrum uncertainty estimates. The spectral library, optimized geometries, and model code are publicly available. They can be used to complement existing libraries for interpreting and modeling JWST AIB observations and those from future IR missions.

CO and [CII], complemented by dust continuum and molecular-gas kinematics, will measure the molecular gas reservoir, its physical conditions, and its dynamical state. Together with JWST and the ELT, ALMA2040 will connect cold gas, dust, and stellar structures across cosmic time. item.title: How Little Red Dots Turn Blue: Evolution of Kelvin-Helmholtz Contracting Black Hole Envelopes and Observational Diagnostics
item.description:

James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations have revealed compact, red-colored, broad-line emitters known as little red dots (LRDs), while a bluer counterpart population has been referred to as little blue dots (LBDs). Their physical connection remains unclear: they may represent different evolutionary stages of the same phenomenon, distinct populations, or different phases of the broader evolution of early galaxies and their black holes (BHs). We propose a model in which a rapidly growing BH is embedded in a geometrically thick gaseous envelope accompanied by concurrent nuclear star formation. The model reproduces the observed spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of LRDs and LBDs, and naturally connects the two phases through Kelvin-Helmholtz contraction of the envelope and exposure of the nuclear accretion disk, as the gas supply declines due to external stellar activity or feedback. We predict the corresponding evolutionary tracks in the UV-optical slope (β_UV-β_opt) plane which bridge the apparent gap between LRDs and LBDs. These evolutionary tracks start from the LRD regime and consistently exhibit a red excursion that extends toward (β_UV,β_opt)~(2,-1) before turning toward the LBD regime. This feature is largely insensitive to variations in the model parameters that govern the envelope structure, providing a robust signature of the transitional population. The transition lasts ~5-50 Myr, depending primarily on the BH feedback efficiency and the gas-retention efficiency of the envelope. The abundance ratio of transitional systems to LRDs therefore provides a constraint on BH feedback and gas retention during the rapid growth of early supermassive BHs.

item.title: A Vision for Little Red Dots in the Low-Redshift Universe with ALMA2040
item.description:
Fengwu Sun, Xiaojing Lin, Miguel Pereira-Santaella, Dieu D. Nguyen

The discovery of Little Red Dots (LRDs) at high redshifts with JWST has revealed a previously unknown phase of black-hole growth. However, their black-hole (BH) masses, BH-to-stellar mass ratios, cold-gas reservoirs, and depletion times remain uncertain. The recent discovery of low-redshift LRDs at z≃0.1 - 0.9 creates a decisive opportunity to access their low-J CO lines for measuring molecular gas reservoirs, and the nearest systems can in principle be spatially resolved. We use J1025+1402 ("The Egg") at z=0.1007, the best-studied local LRD, as a benchmark to explore the scientific opportunities with ALMA2040. Assuming a molecular gas mass of 10^9 M⊙, the CO(2-1) detectability strongly depends on the assumed CO-to-H2 conversion (α_CO). With a large α_CO ≃ 315 - 725 M⊙ (K km s-1 pc^2)^-1 at a low gas-phase metallicity, the CO line would remain very challenging for the current ALMA to detect, while ALMA2040 will likely deliver a robust CO detection and thus a gas-reservoir constraint for The Egg. Furthermore, with the best angular resolution at its CO(2-1) frequency (14.6 mas, or 27 pc), ALMA2040 may spatially resolve the CO emission from The Egg. Assuming an optimistic, SMC-like α_CO with a 50-hour deep integration, we produce mock position-velocity diagrams that may distinguish a 10^7 M⊙ black hole from the no-BH model through its steeper central velocity structure. We conclude that ALMA2040 has the potential to directly measure the gas masses, depletion times, and excitation of local LRDs, while the CO-bright subset may ultimately yield dynamical constraints on the mass of their central black holes.

item.title: Cosmology with strong gravitational lenses
item.description:
Tommaso Treu

Three of the most pressing open questions in cosmology – the nature of dark energy and dark matter, and the growing tension in the value of the Hubble constant H_0 – call for cosmological probes that are independent of, and complementary to, traditional methods. Strong gravitational lensing offers exactly that: a purely gravitational probe of the universe's expansion history and matter distribution, sensitive to dark matter's presence regardless of whether it interacts with light. Time-delay lenses and multiplane lenses can measure H_0 and the dark energy equation of state directly, while the distortion of lensed images can reveal the abundance and internal structure of dark matter subhalos. After a brief theoretical and historical introduction, I review recent breakthroughs enabled by JWST and by advances in lens modeling and stellar dynamics. Examples include the recent measurement of H_0 with 3% precision in flat Λ cold dark matter cosmology, and a tentative detection of dark matter self-interaction. Strong lensing is entering a pivotal era: wide-field surveys with Euclid, Rubin, and Roman, and radio surveys with the Square Kilometer Array, are poised to increase the number of known strong lenses by orders of magnitude, positioning strong lensing to play a central role in answering these open questions in the decade ahead.

item.description:

With the rapid discovery of z>6 galaxies by JWST and lack of constraints on the properties of dust at these redshifts, we must turn to theoretical models to predict the properties of dust at these redshifts. The vast majority of our attenuation curves also lack the 2175 Angstrom absorption feature. Our attenuation laws do not evolve strongly over z=15-5, which we attribute to relatively constant fractions of small grains up to z=4 in our simulations. We present a set of simulation-informed priors on dust attenuation law parameterization that could be implemented in SED fitting codes. There is an anti-correlation between galaxy mass and attenuation curve slope and positive correlation between galaxy mass and A_V, which we attribute to dust growth becoming efficient in our massive galaxies with logM_*/M⊙≳9 and with ISM conditions above a critical metallicity threshold.

While prominent hot H2 emission (≳ 1000 K) has been explored in nearby galaxies, its excitation mechanisms at higher redshifts remain poorly constrained. The H2 line luminosities of the sample show a sublinear dependence on radio luminosity, while the relation between the H2 luminosities and total infrared luminosities is approximately linear after excluding the radio-excess sources. These scaling relations suggest that star formation provides a baseline contribution to hot H2 excitation, while radio-excess sources require an additional contribution from AGN-related processes such as jet- or wind-driven shocks. These results reveal a multi-channel excitation scenario and shed new light on the interplay between star formation, AGN activity, and the interstellar medium during galaxy evolution.

item.title: Galactic Outflows and Star-Formation Quenching: A JWST Perspective
item.description:
Rebecca L. Davies, Sirio Belli

Outflows driven by active galactic nuclei (AGN) are widely considered a key mechanism for regulating and quenching star formation in massive galaxies. However, direct observational evidence linking outflows to quenching has remained elusive for decades. This article reviews recent findings for massive galaxies at cosmic noon (z~ 2), based on sensitive James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations tracing both star formation histories (through Balmer absorption lines) and neutral outflows (through blueshifted NaID absorption). Neutral outflows are found in ~ 25 - 50% of massive (log(M_*/M⊙)> 10) galaxies, independent of star formation rate. Outflows from star-forming galaxies are consistent with being powered by star-formation and/or AGN activity, whereas outflows from quiescent systems are generally attributed to current or previous AGN activity. There is growing evidence that recent rapid quenching of star-formation is associated with powerful AGN-driven outflows with mass loading factors η≳ 1 - 10. The neutral gas dominates the outflow mass budget but in most cases its velocity is below the halo escape velocity, indicating that this gas may form part of a galactic fountain. Detections of neutral gas inflows and residual cold gas reservoirs in quiescent galaxies suggest that other feedback mechanisms such as AGN heating are required to keep galaxies quenched over long timescales. We highlight the potential of multiphase outflow measurements to constrain feedback models, describe the main systematic uncertainties in mass outflow rate measurements, and discuss how the z~ 2 results inform our understanding of the formation of the earliest massive quiescent galaxies.

item.title: How JWST is Revolutionizing Our View of Early Galaxy Formation
item.description:
Rychard Bouwens

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has been revolutionizing our understanding of early galaxy formation over its first four years of science operations. With un- precedented sensitivity, spatial resolution, and wavelength coverage from the near- to mid-infrared, JWST has enabled astronomers to identify hundreds of star-forming galaxies at redshifts z>~8 (within ~650 million years of the Big Bang) through strong spectral breaks and characterize these galaxies through sensitive spectroscopy. These capabilities have provided new insights into the stellar populations, neutral gas, nebular continuum emission, chemical enrichment, dust content, and ionization conditions of galaxies during cosmic dawn, revealing more numerous and brighter systems than anticipated from pre-JWST models. We discuss the implications of these discoveries for reionization, the buildup of stellar mass and metals, and the evolution of galaxy populations and luminosity functions. JWST is also revealing a new physical picture of early galaxies, characterized by compact, clumpy star formation, high gas fractions, and intense radiation fields. Despite much progress, many open questions remain, including the efficiency, intermittency, and stellar initial mass function (IMF) of early star formation, conditions in the interstellar medium (ISM), masses, and structure of the earliest galaxies, and the topology of reionization. Resolving these open questions will require lensing magnification, sensitive spectroscopy to > 5 micron, including with the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA), exploration to higher redshifts, and larger, more complete samples, helping to clarify how the first galaxies formed and evolved.

item.title: Massive black holes in the first billion years with JWST
item.description:
Hannah Übler

The James Webb Space Telescope has unlocked uncharted territory for the study of early black holes, enabling the detection of fainter and smaller black holes at larger cosmological distances than previously possible. Compared to nearby massive black holes, they are characterised by several unexpected attributes, such as their multi-wavelength properties or their relation to their host galaxies. These observational findings challenge our understanding of the past evolution of present-day supermassive black holes, and provide novel anchor points to constrain theoretical models of black hole formation and growth. This review summarises our current understanding of the observed properties of newly discovered, active black holes in the early Universe, discusses the status of mass measurements and the relation to their hosts, as well as open questions and future prospects.

item.title: Extinction by non-spherical particles with the Nanoparticle Transition Matrix Code: perspectives for interstellar medium and exoplanetary atmospheres
item.description:
G. La Mura, G. Mulas, M. A. Iatì, C. Cecchi-Pestellini, G. Aresu, S. Rezaei, R. Saija

The Transition Matrix formalism (T-matrix) offers an optimal solution to the problem of radiation scattering and absorption by particles characterized by a high degree of chemical and structural complexity. However, its application to particle models composed by large numbers of constituents has been classically limited by the substantial computational burden of the method. As a consequence, the investigation of light scattering and absorption processes, in cases where particle asymmetry and non-homogeneity play an important role, typically need to rely on simplifying assumptions which affect the correct interpretation of transmission spectra and extinction curves. This problem has a huge impact on many fields of scientific application. In particular, it has a critical role in astrophysics, because the ability to model highly non homogeneous particles is a fundamental requirement to understand the role of extinction in different phases of the interstellar medium (ISM), as well as to probe the physics of light transmission in planetary atmospheres within the Solar System and beyond. In this work we describe the application of a new implementation of the T-matrix formalism, based on the framework originally developed by Borghese, Denti & Saija and named Nano-particle Transition Matrix code, which leverages the power of modern hardware architectures to reduce the computational costs related to the solution of relevant particle models for the investigation of dust in the ISM and of hot-Jupyter class planets atmospheric aerosols. This new implementation of the T-matrix formalism can handle calculations of increasing complexity with a direct impact in the interpretation of the transmission spectra of transiting exoplanets produced by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and of those expected from the Atmospheric Remote-sensing Infrared Exoplanet Large survey (ARIEL).

item.title: Anisotropic Radiation in Super-Eddington Active Galactic Nuclei: The Responsivity of Broad-Line Regions to Continuum Variability
item.description:
Feng-Na Fang, Pu Du, Jian-Min Wang

Anisotropic ionizing radiation is a natural theoretical expectation for super-Eddington accretion in active galactic nuclei (AGNs), implying that the ionizing flux incident on the broad-line region (BLR) clouds differs from that measured along the observer's line of sight. Reverberation mapping studies have revealed systematically shortened time lags of the broad Hβ emission line relative to continuum variations in super-Eddington AGNs, a phenomenon that can be naturally interpreted as a consequence of anisotropic ionizing continuum radiation. To further investigate this anisotropy, we perform a systematic analysis of the Hβ line responsivity, defined as the ratio of the variability amplitude of Hβ to that of the driving continuum, for both sub- and super-Eddington AGNs. By combining the effective responsivities measured relative to the driving continuum, after correcting for the continuum–emission-line delay, with photoionization calculations, we infer the ionizing radiation field received by their BLRs. We find that, in super-Eddington AGNs, the ionizing flux inferred from the Hβ responsivity differs significantly from that observed along the line of sight, whereas the two are in closer agreement in sub-Eddington AGNs. These results provide compelling evidence for strong anisotropy of the incident ionizing radiation in super-Eddington AGNs. We conclude by discussing the broader implications of this anisotropy, including its potential relevance to the "little red dots" recently discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope.

item.title: When dust growth takes over: the origin of dust in post-reionization galaxies

The physical processes responsible for such rapid dust enrichment remain uncertain. We investigate the dust enrichment history of the ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST (ACJ) sample using the semi-analytic galaxy formation model GAlaxy Evolution and Assembly (GAEA), which follows galaxy assembly, chemical enrichment, and dust evolution. We select model galaxies matching the observed stellar masses, star formation rates, and metallicities of the ACJ sample, compare their dust properties with observed scaling relations, and trace their enrichment histories and environments. The model reproduces the observed dust mass-stellar mass relation and the dust-to-stellar mass, dust-to-gas, and dust-to-metal ratios as functions of stellar mass and metallicity. Reproducing these constraints requires efficient dust growth in the interstellar medium; stellar dust production alone cannot account for the observed dust reservoirs, even under the most optimistic assumptions. The combination of stellar mass, star formation rate, and metallicity provides a good predictor of galaxy dust content. Our model suggests rapid dust build-up consistent with the previously noted rapid metal enrichment, with evidence for a transition around z~8-9 below which dust growth becomes the dominant dust formation channel. Finally, ACJ-like galaxies preferentially reside in locally overdense environments, suggesting that environment may have contributed to their accelerated evolution. Taken together, these results support rapid and coupled stellar, metal, and dust build-up in ACJ galaxies during the post-reionization era.

item.title: ACORN I. Massive Black Hole Seeding and Tidal Disruption Events from Star Clusters in Cosmological Simulations
item.description:
Yihao Zhou, Tiziana Di Matteo, Claire E. Williams, Aklant Kumar Bhowmick, Marta Reina-Campos, Carl L. Rodriguez, Elena González Prieto, Laura Blecha, Rupert Croft

JWST has revealed massive star clusters at z≳ 6, which provide promising environments for massive black hole (MBH) seed formation. We introduce a new MBH seeding model for cosmological simulations, physically motivated by the runaway collisions in star clusters. Subgrid star clusters are generated according to the local ISM and evolved through stellar evolution and two-body relaxation. The masses of MBH seeds formed through runaway collisions are determined by the properties of their host clusters, including the effects of metallicity-dependent stellar winds. We further follow tidal disruption events (TDEs) with the evolving clusters, which can be enhanced in MBH binaries, and account for gravitational-wave (GW) recoil following MBH mergers. We implement this model in a constrained simulation of a 5σ overdense region, where seeds of 10^3-10^5.6 M⊙ form in clusters with 10^4≤ m_SC≤ 10^8 M⊙. Because both the seed abundance and mass are directly connected to the local environment, we have a more physical M_BH\!-\!M_galaxy scaling for low-mass galaxies (M_galaxy~10^6-9 M⊙), a regime poorly described by previous seeding models. Multiple MBHs are naturally allowed to form in-situ within individual halos, producing a spatially clustered population. This increases the MBH merger rate by ~100 relative to other seeding models, significantly enhancing the expected LISA event rate. TDEs can dominate the growth of 10^3-4 M⊙ MBHs and produce luminous flares of L_peak~ 10^42-43 erg s-1, increasing the observability of low-mass seeds. This seeding prescription accelerates early MBH growth at z≳ 8, while subsequent self-regulated gas accretion drives the central MBH toward similar masses ~10^8.6 M⊙ by z=6 across different seeding models.

JWST/NIRCam imaging has enabled efficient selection of a large number of galaxy candidates at very high redshifts. Accurate and robust selection is crucial for statistical analyses, such as measurement of the ultraviolet luminosity function (UV LF). We report the highest-redshift source in CAPERS as UDS-111893 at zspec=12.98, with no sources confirmed at z>13. item.title: Too many or too bright? Status and perspectives in the study of the UV Luminosity Function at z>10
item.description:
A. Fontana, H. Atek, V. Bromm, A. J. Bunker, M. Castellano, P. Dayal, F. D'Eugenio, D. Elbaz, A. Ferrara, S. L. Finkelstein, S. Fujimoto, M. Giavalisco, Y. Harikane, C. Kobayashi, F. Pacucci, P. G. Pérez-González, P. Rosati, A. Trinca, R. Tripodi, P. Santini, E. Vanzella, A. Venditti, A. Weibel

The finding that galaxies in the first 500Myr were much more numerous and/or brighter than expected is often cited as one of the main discoveries of the James Webb Space Telescope in its first four years of operation. This result is now solidly based on an impressive number of surveys that have detected, spectroscopically confirmed, and characterized a relatively large sample of galaxies up to z=14.44, the redshift of the most distant galaxy currently known. This finding has motivated the introduction of additional physical mechanisms into theoretical models to reproduce the observed numbers and luminosities. These results contrast with the failure, despite ongoing efforts, to confirm any galaxy candidate beyond this redshift. This review summarizes the status of the search for and characterization of galaxies at z>9, focusing on the evolution of the UV Luminosity Function (UVLF), which is the main statistical description of the galaxy population that can be obtained at these redshifts. We first provide a comprehensive overview of the full set of JWST data obtained so far. We perform a 'meta–analysis' on the entire data set and provide a simple yet effective description of the global evolution of the UVLF, averaging over the various surveys. We also compare these results extensively with theoretical models that were developed to match the new JWST observations and that explore different physical mechanisms able to drive the observed evolution. We conclude with a summary of the contrasting results regarding the search for galaxy candidates at z>15, and outline the requirements for future surveys aimed at breaking this barrier.

item.title: A New Era for Supernova Science with the James Webb Space Telescope
item.description:

Supernovae (SNe) are excellent probes of the physical, chemical, and cosmological context of galaxies across the history of the Universe. The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST ) has a truly unique combination of wavelength, sensitivity, and resolution, providing a new window into SN physics, progenitors, dust production, redshift evolving stellar populations, and cosmology since its launch. Here we summarize the astounding observations JWST has made of SNe in its first few years of operations, as well as the corresponding advancements in our understanding of the Universe. This includes detailed views of nearby SNe, the first spectroscopic samples of high-z SNe, and a significant number of gravitationally lensed SNe valuable for both cosmological inference and high signal-to-noise (S/N) spectroscopy. While the upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is expected to revolutionize space-based time-domain astronomy, JWST and its unique capabilities will continue to play a complementary role by providing high-precision spectroscopic and photometric data for a broad range of SN science cases.

item.title: Binding Energies of Astrophysically Relevant Molecules on CO<sub>2</sub> Clusters: Benchmarking and the Donor-Acceptor Origin of Surface-Dependent Binding
item.description:
Aneesa Ahmad, Catherine Walsh, Stefan Vogt-Geisse

Carbon dioxide (CO2) is among the most abundant interstellar ices and has been observed by JWST in water-rich mixtures and pure CO2 environments. Astrochemical models adopt binding energies (BEs) measured on water ice because few BEs are available for CO2 ice. We calculate BE distributions for twelve adsorbates (N2, CH_4, HCl, C_2H2, H2S, HF, HCN, H2CO, HCOOH, HNC, CH_3OH, H2O) on CO2 clusters containing two to five molecules using DFT calibrated against CCSD(T)/CBS, a coupled-cluster treatment extrapolated to the complete-basis-set limit. Binding strength depends on whether the adsorbate requires the surface to donate a hydrogen bond (H-bond). CO2 can accept an H-bond but cannot donate one, and all six species compared with water ice from Ahmad et al. (2026) bind more weakly on CO2. The ratio of the BE on CO2 to water ice ranges from 0.66 for H2CO and 0.75 for H2O to 0.87 for CH_3OH, 0.89 for HCOOH and 0.92 for C_2H2. Formaldehyde is predicted to desorb near 57 K from CO2-rich ice, compared with 85 K from water-rich ice, and could contribute to cold gas-phase H2CO. Although the mean binding energies are changing with cluster size for several species, the differences can be traced to local binding interactions likely to remain important in larger ice models. The BEs vary by more than 500 K between sites, while the desorption peaks range from 11 K for CH_4 to 132 K for HCOOH. The limited H-bonding capacity of CO2 may favour separation of mixed H2O:CO2 ice into CO2-rich domains.

item.description:

We use the MUSE-ALMA Haloes sample to build a census of the condensed baryons (stars and cold gas) to study the multiphase interstellar medium and circumgalactic medium (CGM). The sample includes 79 gas-rich galaxies at 0.2<z<1.2 located near strong HI Ly-alpha absorbers along quasar sightlines within projected separations of ~5-270 kpc and radial velocity separations of up to 500 km/s. HST spectroscopy characterises the absorbers, while HST imaging, MUSE and ALMA observations trace the stars, ionised gas and molecular gas. We find the following results. (i) HI masses inferred from optical properties show broad agreement with those derived from the CGM absorber properties for impact parameters <100 kpc, although group environments can significantly influence these estimates. (ii) The molecular gas fraction declines more steeply with stellar mass than the HI fraction. This suggests that stars build up more rapidly than the cold gas reservoir, while massive galaxies either consume their molecular gas more efficiently or convert HI into H2 less efficiently. (iii) Galaxies with high stellar surface densities exhibit the highest baryon fractions. This may reflect baryonic feedback, which can produce flatter inner dark matter profiles in high surface density systems, or aperture effects, where the ionised gas kinematic tracer probes only the innermost, baryon-dominated regions in compact sources, but extends further into the dark matter halo in sources with extended baryonic distributions. (iv) A few galaxies are consistent with being the baryon-dominated descendants of the low mass z~6 galaxies detected by JWST, while many appear to be substantially more dark matter dominated, lower mass systems with progenitors beyond JWST detection limits. This study provides a multiscale, multiphase view of the gas in and around galaxies, allowing us to probe the baryon budget across cosmic time.

item.title: SAGE26 Paper I: Modelling the baryon cycle from cosmic dawn to the present day
item.description:
Michael Bradley, Darren J. Croton, Robert Adriel Mostoghiu Paun, Dhruba Dutta Chowdhury, Jayde Willingham

We present SAGE26, a comprehensive update to the Semi-Analytic Galaxy Evolution (SAGE) model. SAGE26 integrates five observationally motivated improvements: (1) distinct circumgalactic medium and hot-halo gas physics, (2) molecular hydrogen for star formation, (3) velocity- and redshift-dependent supernova feedback, (4) bulge radii tracking through time, and (5) feedback-free burst galaxies. Each improvement works to regulate galaxy formation from cosmic dawn to the present. Most significantly, the addition of feedback-free burst galaxies provides a pathway to produce high-redshift massive galaxies at the abundances observed by the James Webb Space Telescope. Furthermore, the new circumgalactic medium framework improves the treatment of baryons by distinguishing between free-fall-limited inflow in low-mass haloes and hydrostatic cooling in massive groups and clusters using a characteristic halo shock mass. SAGE26 reproduces key observational constraints across cosmic time, including the stellar mass function and cosmic star formation rate density, while retaining the computational efficiency and flexibility of its predecessor. The code and data products are open-source and publicly available.

item.title: Halo Mass Function Constraints on Early Galaxy and AGN Populations in the JWST Era
item.description:
Elan Yogeswaren, Robert Schaefer

The discovery by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) of massive galaxies and luminous active galactic nuclei (AGN) at high redshift provides an increasingly sensitive test of the connection between cosmological structure formation and the astrophysical processes that make dark matter halos observable. We develop a framework connecting the linear matter power spectrum to the mass variance, peak height, halo mass function (HMF), cumulative halo abundance, and observable galaxy and AGN populations. We use the Sheth-Tormen (ST) HMF as the baseline and compare it with an illustrative Bolshoi-Klypin-calibrated modification (KST) to quantify the sensitivity of predictions to the calibration of the HMF against cosmological N-body simulations. We apply the framework to three complementary tests: the baryonic and stellar mass reservoir available to massive galaxies, the abundance of halos capable of hosting luminous AGN, and the rest frame ultraviolet luminosity function of high redshift galaxies. Because the most massive systems occupy the rare, high peak tail of the halo distribution, modest changes in inferred host mass, baryonic conversion efficiency, black-hole occupation or duty cycle, and HMF calibration can produce large changes in predicted abundances. The ST-KST comparison shows that uncertainty in the high redshift halo population can materially affect the inferred host supply, particularly toward large z (10). Comparison with representative JWST massive galaxy, AGN, and UV luminosity function measurements demonstrates that matching the properties of an individual source is not sufficient for population consistency; the corresponding host halos must also exist in adequate numbers. Current observations provide increasingly stringent quantitative stress tests of both cosmological halo abundances and the baryonic and black hole physics at cosmic dawn.

Two scenarios are usually invoked to explain their existence – genuine physical structures or resolution-driven artifacts – yet distinguishing between them requires characterizing their internal structure. In this work, part of the Star-Forming Clumps As Layered Emergent Structures (SCALES) series, we hence ask: What is inside a giant clump? Characterizing giant clump stellar mass composition using the most massive member clump and the remaining constituent clumps, we find it consistent with random sampling of the host galaxy's clump population, and hence the clump stellar mass function. This conclusion agrees qualitatively with both prevailing scenarios – (I) dominant long-lived giant clumps, although requiring constant renewal of their constituents, and (II) giant clumps as mere blended clump associations. However, most models make no strong claims about their internal mass distribution beyond order-of-magnitude statements, and our observations thus provide an empirical constraint against which such models can be re-evaluated. Finally, using the total mass budget of clumps and ECs, we find that the clump stellar mass function cannot be described by a single power law of slope ≈ 2, but requires a break to a shallower slope at ~ 10^7.4 M⊙.

item.title: Separating the Optical to Near-Infrared Light of AGN and Their Host Galaxies
item.description:
Callum Dewsnap, Pauline Barmby, Sarah C. Gallagher

The properties of galaxies that host active galactic nuclei (AGNs) offer clues to the conditions that enable accretion onto supermassive black holes. A galaxy's morphology can provide significant information on the evolutionary processes underway. By modeling the surface-brightness profiles of galaxies that host AGN, we can characterize physical properties of the host galaxy. With a sample of sources across a wide range of redshifts, we can investigate how both the supermassive black hole and galaxy evolve over time. Applying the best practices from previous work, we perform Sersic + point source fits of 96 X-ray-selected AGN in the Extended Groth Strip across up to 13 bands of James Webb Space Telescope and Hubble Space Telescope imaging using AstroPhot. We examine both parametric (Sersic) and nonparametric methods in tandem to best determine the physical properties of the host galaxy. After separating the light of the host galaxy and the AGN, we perform independent CIGALE model fits to photometric spectral energy distributions to estimate physical properties including the host galaxy stellar mass and star formation rate, and AGN disk luminosity. In the stellar-mass/star-formation-rate plane, the AGN host galaxies align with the population of massive non-AGN galaxies in the control sample across all redshifts. The AGN disk luminosities result in ratios of bolometric to X-ray flux within the expected range, 5-20:1. We provide an evaluation of the limitations of Sersic modeling to obtain galaxy properties and provide recommendations on best practices for multi-band AGN+host galaxy image decomposition with James Webb Space Telescope imaging.

item.title: Probing the Reionization History and Bubble Sizes with JWST Lyman-α Fraction Measurements
item.description:
Aritra Kundu, Adam Lidz, Guochao Sun

Recent James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) measurements quantify the fraction of ultraviolet-selected galaxies showing detectable Lyman-alpha (Ly-α) lines at z ~ 6-14. These Ly-α fractions are partly shaped by Ly-α scattering from neutral hydrogen in the surrounding intergalactic medium (IGM), and so the observed Ly-α fraction evolution can inform our understanding of the reionization history and the size distribution of ionized bubbles during reionization. We compare the JWST measurements with Ly-α transmission calculations based on both the THESAN reionization simulations and a flexible semi-analytic model. In each case, we calibrate a sub-grid model for the intrinsic Ly-α emission lines emerging from the interstellar medium (ISM) and circumgalactic medium (CGM) of the host galaxies using empirical estimates of the Ly-α equivalent width (EW) distributions at z ~ 6. We find that the reionization history and bubble sizes in THESAN yield good agreement with current JWST Ly-α fraction observations, with a reduced χ^2_ν= 0.4-1.2. Our semi-analytic models and THESAN Ly-α transmission calculations agree well, allowing us to explore a wide range of reionization models. We derive 1σ bounds on the average mass-weighted neutral fractions of: ⟨ x_HI ⟩ = 0.38^+0.14_-0.38 (0.52^+0.09_-0.21), 0.57^+0.23_-0.57 (0.68^+0.12_-0.39), and 0.93^+0.05_-0.17 (0.89^+0.11_-0.15) at z ~ 7, 8, and 11, based on the Ly-α fraction measurements with EW >25 \mathringA (>10 \mathringA).

item.title: Sub-kiloparsec Test of the Kennicutt-Schmidt Relation in a Strongly Lensed Dusty Star-Forming Galaxy at z~2.78
item.description:
C. Cornil-Baïotto, J. Molina, G. Mahler, G. Rihtaršič, M. Boquien, M. Bradač, E. Ibar, A. H. Gonzalez, T. Verdugo, O. López-Cruz, J. Magaña, V. Motta

[abridged] Star formation is a key process driving galaxy evolution, but understanding how it proceeds within the interstellar medium (ISM) requires resolving cold molecular gas and dust on sub-kpc scales. At z~2-3, near the peak of cosmic star formation, such resolution can generally only be achieved through strong gravitational lensing. We present an ALMA study of SMMJ0658, a 20x-magnified main-sequence star-forming galaxy at z=2.7768 +/- 0.0002, lensed by the Bullet Cluster (z=0.296) into three images. We use 0.2" and 0.6" ALMA Band-3 observations to test the Kennicutt-Schmidt (KS) relation at sub-kpc scales at cosmic noon. Using a JWST-based strong-lensing model of the Bullet Cluster, we reconstruct source-plane CO(3-2) and rest-frame 803um dust-continuum maps down to ~200pc scales. We derive spatially resolved molecular gas and star formation rate surface densities, depletion times, and the scale dependence of the CO-to-dust flux ratio over 200pc-3.2kpc apertures. The 0.2" ALMA data reveal massive, dense star-forming clumps, with Sigma_mol ~1.3-2.3 x 10^3 M_sun pc^-2, Sigma_SFR ~0.5-2.3 M_sun yr^-1 kpc^-2, and tau_dep ~0.82-2.56 Gyr. CO-dust spatial decorrelation produces a strong scale dependence in tau_dep. We find a KS-relation breakdown scale of 0.8 +/- 0.1 kpc, consistent with individual regions tracing distinct stages of the star-formation cycle. The ALMA and JWST data also reveal evidence for a lensed galaxy pair at z~2.78, although whether SMMJ0658 is undergoing an early-stage interaction remains uncertain. Our results show that the apparent universality of the KS relation breaks down once individual star-forming regions are spatially resolved, in line with observations from the local universe to z~1. We extend this picture to z~2.78, providing new insight into the resolved properties of the clumpy cold ISM and the star-formation cycle at cosmic noon.

item.title: Cosmic Collisions I: Optical Morphologies for MIRI-selected galaxies from the PRIMER survey
item.description:
Gregory Troiani, Allison Kirkpatrick, Leyna Bajaj, Joseph Havens, Jackson Stephens, Anton M. Koekemoer, James S. Dunlop, Adriano Fontana, Norman Grogin, Pablo G. Pérez-González

We present the first results of visual morphology classifications from the Cosmic Collisions project, comprising 14,657 galaxies from the JWST Public Release IMaging for Extragalactic Research (PRIMER) survey. The sample consists of galaxies detected with MIRI F770W and spans the epoch of peak cosmic star formation (1<z<3). We produce rest-frame optical and observed-frame mid-IR images and enlisted citizen science volunteers through the Zooniverse platform to classify galaxy morphology, surface features, and interactions. The project accumulated 304,524 classifications from more than 4,700 volunteers. We find that mid-IR selected galaxies have significantly different morphologies relative to optical and near-IR selected galaxies, favoring dust-rich disk galaxies at z<2 and compact systems at z>2. This inverts findings from optical selection, which shows galaxies becoming more bulge-dominated and elliptical over cosmic time. In addition, we identify a population of galaxies with disk-like optical morphologies and luminous mid-IR point-source cores that may represent obscured AGN candidates, offering a promising path to identify AGNs based on imaging alone. Comparison with visual classifications from HST imaging demonstrates the impact of JWST's improved sensitivity and resolution on the identification of galaxy structure and interactions, with systems previously identified by HST as compact, smooth, or featureless showing significant extended and internal structure in JWST. These results provide a foundation for future investigations into the connection between morphology, dust structure, star formation, and AGN activity.

AT 2026abck was detected on 2026 Aug 7 in NIRCam F200W imaging, with contemporaneous detection from parallel NIRCam F150W+F277W imaging.
